title: Schopenhauer
orientation: Russell presents Schopenhauer as a genuine oddity among philosophers: an unrelenting pessimist in an overwhelmingly optimistic tradition, who adapted Kant's philosophy by retaining and radicalizing the 'thing-in-itself' (identifying it with Will) rather than discarding it as Fichte and Hegel had done. The chapter covers Schopenhauer's life, his metaphysics of a single, evil, cosmic Will underlying all appearance, his doctrine of ascetic resignation drawn from Hinduism and Buddhism as the only escape from suffering, and Russell's sharp final judgment that Schopenhauer's own comfortable, quarrelsome, and self-indulgent life sits very awkwardly with the philosophy of renunciation he preached.
historical_background: Schopenhauer (1788-1860) was born in Danzig to a prosperous, Voltairian, Anglophile merchant father who moved the family to Hamburg rather than live under Prussian annexation, and a literary mother who kept a salon in Weimar. Russell notes Schopenhauer's cosmopolitan upbringing (extensive time in France and England) made him unusually free of the German nationalism found in Fichte and Hegel. He briefly and unsuccessfully competed with Hegel for lecture audiences at Berlin, retreated into private life in Dresden, and did not receive significant recognition until near the end of his life, decades after his principal work, The World as Will and Idea (1818), was published.
philosophical_problems: Is the world, at bottom, good, evil, or indifferent -- and is pessimism or optimism the more defensible philosophical temperament?
What is the relationship between Kant's 'thing-in-itself' and the human will, and can retaining the thing-in-itself (rather than discarding it, as Fichte and Hegel did) yield a coherent metaphysics?
If suffering is essential to existence, what -- if anything -- can be done to escape or reduce it, and is asceticism a coherent response?
Should will or knowledge be regarded as metaphysically and ethically fundamental?

philosophers_discussed.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's primary subject: his life, his adaptation of Kant's philosophy into a metaphysics of Will, his pessimism, his doctrine of ascetic resignation drawn from Hinduism and Buddhism, and the marked gap between his philosophy and his personal conduct are all examined.

philosophers_discussed.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as the primary source of Schopenhauer's system: Schopenhauer retains Kant's 'thing-in-itself' (which Fichte and Hegel had abandoned) and, building on Kant's linkage of the moral law to the will, identifies the thing-in-itself with Will itself.

philosophers_discussed.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as a lecturer Schopenhauer heard at Berlin and 'despised'; contrasted with Schopenhauer as one of the philosophers who discarded the thing-in-itself and thereby made knowledge, rather than will, metaphysically fundamental.

core_concepts.name: The world as Will
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Schopenhauer argues that what appears to us, in perception, as our own body is really, in its inner nature, our will; and since space and time (which are what make things separate and many) belong only to appearance and not to ultimate reality, this will cannot really be many separate individual wills -- it must be a single, timeless, universal Will underlying the whole of nature, animate and inanimate alike.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Schopenhauer's central metaphysical claim, developed from Kant: the 'thing-in-itself' (retained, unlike in Fichte and Hegel) is identical with Will; since time and space (Kant's 'principle of individuation') belong only to phenomena, the thing-in-itself/Will cannot be plural or composed of discrete acts of will, and is therefore one, timeless, and identical with the will of the whole universe, of which individual selfhood is merely an illusion of subjective, spatio-temporal perception.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the foundation of Schopenhauer's whole system, and represents, in Russell's assessment, a more defensible development of certain genuine strands in Kant (the connection of the moral law and the thing-in-itself to volition) than most Kantians acknowledged.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea (1818).
examples: Schopenhauer's claim that 'what appears to perception as my body is really my will'
The kept poodle named 'Atma' (world-soul), reflecting Schopenhauer's Hindu-influenced monism
competing_positions: Fichte's and Hegel's abandonment of the thing-in-itself, making knowledge (not will) metaphysically fundamental
Spinoza's pantheism, which Schopenhauer's cosmic-will doctrine initially resembles but then diverges from sharply via pessimism
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly inaugurates the 'primacy of will' tradition Russell traces through Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Draws explicitly on Hindu and Buddhist metaphysics (the veil of Maya, the illusion of individuation).

core_concepts.name: Cosmic pessimism: Will as evil
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Unlike thinkers who might identify the one universal Will with God and urge conformity to it (as Spinoza does), Schopenhauer holds the Will itself is wicked -- the very source of all suffering -- since willing has no fixed end that, once achieved, would bring lasting contentment; unfulfilled desire causes pain, and even satisfied desire brings only fleeting satiety before the cycle begins again.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Schopenhauer's ethical verdict on the metaphysical Will: it is the source of all suffering, since it is essentially endless striving without any final satisfaction, such that 'there is no such thing as happiness, for an unfulfilled wish causes pain, and attainment brings only satiety'; suffering is thus not accidental but essential to all life and is increased, not decreased, by increased knowledge.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is what makes Schopenhauer, unusually among voluntarist philosophers, a pessimist -- a combination Russell calls 'only possible for a pessimist,' since most later thinkers who prioritized will (e.g. Nietzsche) found in it grounds for optimism instead.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea.
examples: The soap-bubble image: 'we blow out a soap-bubble as long and as large as possible, although we know perfectly well that it will burst'
Shame associated with the sexual act, since procreation creates new occasions for suffering and death
objections: Russell: 'From a scientific point of view, optimism and pessimism are alike objectionable: optimism assumes... that the universe exists to please us, and pessimism that it exists to displease us. Scientifically, there is no evidence that it is concerned with us either one way or the other.'
competing_positions: The predominant optimistic temperament Russell says has been 'much commoner among Western philosophers'
Later voluntarists (Nietzsche, Bergson) who affirm will without Schopenhauer's pessimism
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell credits Schopenhauer's pessimism with a historically useful function: making it possible 'for men to take to philosophy without having to persuade themselves that all evil can be explained away.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Leads directly to Schopenhauer's preference for Buddhism and Hinduism over Christianity.

core_concepts.name: The veil of Maya and ascetic salvation (Nirvana)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Schopenhauer holds that the distinctness of one person from another is only an illusion ('the veil of Maya'); a good or wise person sees through this illusion via sympathy/love, recognizes that all suffering is ultimately one, and responds by turning away from willing altogether -- through complete chastity, voluntary poverty, fasting, and self-denial -- aiming at something like Buddhist Nirvana, which Schopenhauer interprets as extinction.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Schopenhauer's soteriology: since suffering results from the intensity of will, and the separateness of individuals is merely phenomenal (the 'veil of Maya'), the path to relief from suffering lies in the good man's loving, sympathetic insight into the unity of all things, which quiets and eventually denies his own will; practised fully (through asceticism, chastity, and self-torture), this leads toward a state Schopenhauer calls Nirvana, interpreted as the extinction of individual willing and, ultimately, of the phenomenal world itself as objectified will.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Schopenhauer's proposed 'way out' of cosmic suffering, explicitly modeled on Hindu and Buddhist doctrine rather than Christian doctrine, which he holds in generally low regard (though he still admires Christian mystics like Eckhart and the Christian doctrine of original sin).
core_concepts.historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea, Book IV; explicitly credited by Schopenhauer to Kant, Plato, and the Upanishads.
examples: Schopenhauer's ranking of Buddhism as 'the highest religion'
His hostility to what he calls the 'detestable doctrine of Islam'
The claim that after complete abolition of will, 'this our world... is nothing'
objections: Russell: it is 'not very consistent and not very sincere,' since the mystics Schopenhauer invokes sought positive union with God through contemplation, while Schopenhauer offers only a wholly negative goal (near-nonexistence), an interpretation Russell calls 'an insult to the mystics.'

Russell: so long as the sage exists at all, he still possesses will (which is evil), so he can only diminish, never eliminate, evil while alive -- making the doctrine's promised 'salvation' incoherent short of actual death, which Schopenhauer nonetheless says suicide cannot achieve.

Russell notes the doctrine is undercut by Schopenhauer's own life: he 'habitually dined well,' had many trivial love affairs, was quarrelsome and avaricious, and once threw an elderly seamstress downstairs, causing permanent injury and a court-ordered payment for the rest of her life.
competing_positions: Christian mysticism's positive goal of union with God, which Russell contrasts with Schopenhauer's purely negative 'nothingness'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Helped popularize Hindu and Buddhist ideas among European artistic and literary audiences.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicit and extensive engagement with Hindu, Buddhist, and Christian religious doctrine as rival paths to salvation.

core_concepts.name: The primacy of Will over Knowledge
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Where much earlier philosophy (and ordinary common sense) treats reason or knowledge as what is most fundamentally 'us,' Schopenhauer argues that will -- desire, striving, volition -- is metaphysically prior to and more fundamental than knowledge or intellect.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Schopenhauer's doctrine, historically independent of his pessimism, that will is metaphysically paramount over knowledge/intellect; Russell judges this -- not the pessimism -- to be Schopenhauer's more historically important contribution, since it was 'prepared by Rousseau and Kant, but was first proclaimed in its purity by Schopenhauer,' inaugurating what Russell calls 'the most notable change that has come over the temper of philosophy in our age.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It set the template later followed, in far more optimistic forms, by Nietzsche, Bergson, William James, and Dewey, marking a broad philosophical shift away from treating knowledge as paramount.
core_concepts.historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea.
examples: Schopenhauer's inversion of the ordinary view: the body is the appearance of which will, not knowledge, is the underlying reality
competing_positions: The rationalist and empiricist traditions that treat knowledge/reason as metaphysically or ethically fundamental
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly named by Russell as influencing Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey, 'in one form or another.'

arguments.title: The argument from Kant's ethics to Will as the thing-in-itself
premises: Kant held that a study of the moral law gives us knowledge behind mere phenomena, i.e. knowledge of the world of things-in-themselves.

Kant held the moral law is essentially concerned with the will, and that the difference between a good and a bad man is a difference in the world of things-in-themselves as well as a difference of volition.
Therefore, for Kant, volitions must belong to the real world (things-in-themselves), not merely to the world of phenomena.
The phenomenon corresponding to a volition is a bodily movement.
arguments.conclusion: The body is the appearance (phenomenon) of which will is the underlying reality (thing-in-itself).
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as a genuinely serious philosophical development of Kant -- 'more to be said for this view as a development of Kant than most Kantians were willing to recognize' -- distinguishing it from the more casual abandonment of the thing-in-itself by Fichte and Hegel.
implications: Since time and space belong only to phenomena on Kant's view, and Schopenhauer accepts this, it follows that the will (as thing-in-itself) cannot be dated or composed of separate acts, and must be one, timeless, and identical with the will of the whole universe.

arguments.title: The argument from essential dissatisfaction to universal suffering
premises: Will has no fixed end which, if achieved, would bring lasting contentment.
Attainment of a wish brings only satiety, not lasting happiness.
arguments.conclusion: There is no such thing as genuine, lasting happiness; suffering is essential to all life and increases with increased knowledge.
arguments.explanation: This argument grounds Schopenhauer's pessimism and motivates his prescription of ascetic resignation as the only route to relief, since if desire itself (rather than any particular unmet desire) is the source of suffering, only the extinction of desire/will can end suffering.
objections: Russell counters that pessimism, like optimism, is 'a matter of temperament, not of reason' and is scientifically unwarranted, since there is no evidence the universe is 'concerned with us' to please or displease us.
implications: Leads directly to Schopenhauer's doctrine that the good man practises complete chastity, voluntary poverty, fasting, and self-torture in order to break down his individual will.

key_distinctions: The thing-in-itself retained (Schopenhauer) vs. abandoned (Fichte, Hegel)
Will (ethically evil, but metaphysically fundamental) vs. Knowledge (metaphysically derivative, but capable of redemptive insight)
The doctrine of evolution of the individuation (space/time as 'principium individuationis') vs. the timeless, singular Will
Schopenhauer's stated philosophy of renunciation vs. his actual, self-indulgent personal conduct
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Schopenhauer explicitly acknowledges three sources: Kant (whose thing-in-itself he retains and radicalizes), Plato (though Russell doubts he owes as much to Plato as he thinks), and the Upanishads (Hindu scripture). He is also placed in contrast with Fichte and Hegel, his immediate contemporaries, who took German idealism in the opposite (anti-thing-in-itself, absolutist) direction.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell identifies Schopenhauer as the historical originator, 'first proclaimed in its purity,' of the primacy-of-will tradition carried forward (in far more optimistic forms) by Nietzsche (treated in the next chapter), Bergson, William James, and Dewey.
political_social_context: Comparatively light in this chapter: Russell notes Schopenhauer's family fled Danzig for Hamburg rather than live under Prussian annexation, his anti-democratic views, and his hostility to the 1848 revolution, but the chapter is centered on metaphysics and ethics rather than politics.
religion_science_culture_context: Extensive engagement with Hinduism and Buddhism as sources of Schopenhauer's doctrine of Nirvana and ascetic resignation, alongside his more qualified admiration for certain elements of Christian doctrine (original sin, mystics like Eckhart and Angelus Silesius) and his outright hostility to Islam and to the New Testament's 'deficient... metaphysics.'
russell_presentation: Russell presents Schopenhauer sympathetically as an intellectually serious and unusually cosmopolitan figure -- 'a man of wide culture,' unusually free of nationalism -- whose adaptation of Kant (retaining the thing-in-itself and identifying it with Will) has more going for it than most Kantians recognized. He reconstructs the metaphysics of the single, timeless, cosmic Will, Schopenhauer's pessimistic verdict that this Will is evil and the source of all suffering, and his prescribed ascetic path to Nirvana drawn from Hindu and Buddhist sources. Russell then turns sharply critical of the coherence and sincerity of this doctrine, arguing it does not match the positive goals of the Christian mystics Schopenhauer invokes, and -- in the chapter's most pointed passage -- contrasts Schopenhauer's preached renunciation with his actually comfortable, quarrelsome, and self-indulgent life, citing the incident in which he threw an elderly seamstress down the stairs and was ordered to pay her a pension. Russell closes by separating Schopenhauer's two historical contributions -- pessimism (useful mainly as a corrective to complacent optimism, but not more 'true' than optimism) and the primacy of will (which Russell regards as the more historically important and influential doctrine, 'the most notable change that has come over the temper of philosophy in our age').
critical_context: Common scholarly note: Russell's biographical attack on Schopenhauer's hypocrisy (his comfortable dining, love affairs, and the seamstress incident) has been echoed by many popular accounts but is sometimes flagged by specialists as an ad hominem that, even if factually accurate, does not by itself refute the philosophical coherence of Schopenhauer's metaphysics of Will, only the sincerity of his personal practice of it. Later development: Schopenhauer's aesthetics (his account of art, and especially music, as offering temporary escape from willing) receives little attention in Russell's chapter despite being central to Schopenhauer's influence on artists and composers (notably Wagner); a student wanting a fuller picture of Schopenhauer's cultural influence should note this is a gap in Russell's presentation, which focuses almost exclusively on the metaphysics of Will and the ethics of renunciation.
key_takeaways: Schopenhauer is unusual among philosophers for combining metaphysical seriousness with unrelenting pessimism, in a tradition (Western philosophy) that Russell says has generally leaned optimistic.
Unlike Fichte and Hegel, Schopenhauer retains Kant's 'thing-in-itself' and identifies it with Will, arguing that what appears to perception as the body is, in reality, will.

Because time and space (the 'principle of individuation') belong only to appearance, Schopenhauer's Will must be single, timeless, and identical with the will of the whole universe -- individual selfhood is illusory.

Schopenhauer holds this cosmic Will is evil, the source of all suffering, since willing has no fixed end that brings lasting satisfaction; only the extinction of will (modeled on Buddhist Nirvana) offers relief.

Russell judges Schopenhauer's ascetic doctrine 'not very consistent and not very sincere,' citing the sharp contrast between his preached renunciation and his actual comfortable, quarrelsome, and self-indulgent life.

Russell regards Schopenhauer's doctrine of the primacy of will over knowledge -- not his pessimism -- as his more historically important legacy, directly influencing Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey.
study_notes:
Schopenhauer's chapter is short but conceptually dense, and its structure rewards being studied as a chain: Kant's thing-in-itself -> Schopenhauer's identification of it with Will -> the argument (from space/time as merely phenomenal) that this Will must be single and timeless -> the further, separable claim that this Will is evil -> the prescribed ascetic response modeled on Hindu/Buddhist doctrine. Keep the second link (Will is single/timeless, an argument from Kantian premises about space and time) analytically separate from the third (Will is evil, a further and independent claim); Russell is explicit that primacy-of-will and pessimism are logically separable, since later voluntarists like Nietzsche affirmed the first while rejecting the second.

When studying Russell's critique, notice that he offers two distinct kinds of objection: an internal, philosophical one (the ascetic doctrine's goal is incoherently negative, offering nothing like the positive mystical union it claims kinship with) and an external, biographical one (Schopenhauer's own conduct contradicts his preaching). These are logically independent -- a hypocrite can still hold a true or coherent philosophy -- and a strong essay answer on this chapter should be able to evaluate them separately rather than treating the biographical material as, by itself, a refutation.

Finally, register Russell's own explicit methodological point about pessimism versus optimism: both, he says, are equally unscientific temperamental commitments, since there is no evidence the universe is 'concerned with us' either way. This even-handed dismissal of both temperaments is worth contrasting with Russell's own generally more optimistic, meliorist political and ethical outlook elsewhere in the book.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Kant's idea of the unknowable reality behind appearances; while Fichte and Hegel dropped this idea, Schopenhauer kept it and claimed it is, in fact, Will.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Kant's noumenal reality underlying phenomena, which Schopenhauer -- unlike Fichte and Hegel, who abandoned it -- retains and identifies with Will, arguing the body is merely its phenomenal appearance.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Schopenhauer's scholastic term for space and time -- the features of experience that make things separate and countable as 'many' rather than 'one.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Schopenhauer's term, adapted from scholastic philosophy, for space and time as the source of plurality/individuation among phenomena; since (per Kant) space and time are merely phenomenal, the underlying Will cannot be individuated and must be single.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Hindu concept Schopenhauer adopts for the illusion that makes us see ourselves as separate from other people and things; seeing through it is the beginning of wisdom and compassion.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Schopenhauer's term (borrowed from Hindu philosophy) for the illusion of individuation and separateness in the phenomenal world; the good man, through sympathetic insight, sees through this veil and recognizes the underlying unity of all suffering beings.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Buddhist term for liberation from suffering, which Schopenhauer interprets specifically as extinction -- the ending of individual will and, ultimately, of the phenomenal world as such.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The goal of Schopenhauer's ascetic path, interpreted as the extinction of will and, with it, of the entire objectified phenomenal world; Russell notes Schopenhauer's own text leaves this goal 'wholly and entirely negative,' with no positive content comparable to Christian mystical union with God.

questions.prompt: What makes Schopenhauer 'peculiar among philosophers,' according to Russell's opening characterization?
questions.answer: He is a pessimist, whereas almost all other philosophers are in some sense optimists; he is only partly academic; he dislikes Christianity and prefers Hindu and Buddhist religion; he is unusually free from nationalism; and he began the emphasis on Will characteristic of much later philosophy, but -- unusually -- treats Will as ethically evil rather than good.
questions.explanation: This opening list frames the whole chapter's structure, moving from biography to metaphysics to ethics.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Schopenhauer's argument, building on Kant, for identifying the body's underlying thing-in-itself with Will.
questions.answer: Kant held that the moral law gives knowledge of things-in-themselves, and that the moral law concerns the will; the difference between a good and bad man is thus a difference both in the world of things-in-themselves and in volition. Therefore volitions must belong to the real (thing-in-itself) world, not merely to phenomena. Since the phenomenon corresponding to a volition is a bodily movement, the body is the appearance of which will is the underlying reality.
questions.explanation: Russell credits this as a serious and underappreciated development of genuine strands within Kant's own philosophy.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Schopenhauer's reasoning as Russell reconstructs it, must the underlying cosmic Will be single and timeless rather than plural and composed of separate acts?
questions.answer: Because, per Kant (whom Schopenhauer follows here), space and time belong only to phenomena and not to the thing-in-itself; since space and time (the 'principle of individuation') are what make things separate and many, the Will -- being the thing-in-itself -- cannot be dated or composed of distinct individual acts of will, and must therefore be one, timeless, and identical with the will of the whole universe.
questions.explanation: This argument is the technical core of Schopenhauer's cosmic monism and explains why individual selfhood is, for him, ultimately illusory.

questions.prompt: What is Russell's scientific objection to Schopenhauer's pessimism (and, symmetrically, to optimism)?
questions.answer: Russell argues that optimism assumes or tries to prove the universe exists to please us, while pessimism assumes it exists to displease us; scientifically, there is no evidence the universe is concerned with human beings either way, so belief in either pessimism or optimism is a matter of temperament, not reason.
questions.explanation: Despite this objection, Russell credits pessimism with historical usefulness as a corrective to complacent philosophical optimism.

questions.prompt: Compare Schopenhauer's doctrine of Nirvana with the goals of the Christian mystics he invokes, as Russell presents the contrast.
questions.answer: The Christian mystics Schopenhauer appeals to believed in contemplation leading to the Beatific Vision, a profound and positive kind of knowledge treated as the supreme good; Christianity likewise teaches that eternal life consists in knowledge of God. Schopenhauer, by contrast, holds that piercing the veil of Maya reveals not God but a wicked, suffering-generating Will, so the sage's goal becomes wholly negative -- the closest approach to non-existence -- which Russell says is 'an insult to the mystics' to conflate with their actually positive aim.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's sharpest internal (philosophical, not biographical) criticisms of Schopenhauer's system.

questions.prompt: What specific biographical incident does Russell cite as evidence that Schopenhauer's doctrine of asceticism was insincere?
questions.answer: Schopenhauer threw an elderly seamstress downstairs after being annoyed by her talking outside his apartment door, causing her permanent injury; she obtained a court order requiring him to pay her a quarterly sum for the rest of her life, and when she finally died after twenty years, he noted in his account-book, 'Obit anus, abit onus' ('The old woman dies, the burden departs').
questions.explanation: Russell uses this alongside Schopenhauer's comfortable dining, trivial love affairs, quarrelsomeness, and avarice to argue his life contradicts his preached doctrine of renunciation and universal sympathy.

questions.prompt: Which later philosophers does Russell name as continuing, in various (generally more optimistic) forms, Schopenhauer's doctrine of the primacy of will over knowledge?
questions.explanation: Russell treats this doctrine, not pessimism, as Schopenhauer's more historically significant legacy, marking 'the most notable change that has come over the temper of philosophy in our age.'

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes Schopenhauer from most other Western philosophers, according to Russell?
options: He was not academically trained at all
He is a pessimist in a largely optimistic tradition
He rejected the existence of Will entirely
quiz.explanation: Russell opens the chapter by noting Schopenhauer's unusual pessimism against a largely optimistic philosophical tradition.

quiz.prompt: Which Kantian concept does Schopenhauer retain, unlike Fichte and Hegel?
quiz.explanation: Schopenhauer keeps the thing-in-itself and identifies it with Will, while Fichte and Hegel abandoned it.

quiz.prompt: True or False: According to Schopenhauer, the cosmic Will is composed of many separate, individual wills that interact with each other in time.
quiz.explanation: Because time and space belong only to phenomena, the Will as thing-in-itself must be single and timeless, not plural or composed of separate acts.

quiz.prompt: What does Schopenhauer identify as the ultimate cause of suffering?

Original sin as taught by the Church

quiz.explanation: Schopenhauer ranks Buddhism as the highest religion, while calling Islam a 'detestable doctrine' and finding the Gospels 'sadly deficient in metaphysics.'

The primacy of will, influencing Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey
Both were rejected entirely by later philosophers
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly separates the two doctrines and credits the primacy-of-will thesis, not pessimism, with being 'the most notable change that has come over the temper of philosophy in our age.'
quiz.related_concept: The primacy of Will over Knowledge

Pessimism was invented only in the nineteenth century
quiz.explanation: Russell treats optimism and pessimism as symmetrically unscientific temperamental commitments, since neither is evidenced by the universe's actual indifference to human concerns.

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Schopenhauer's argument, as reconstructed from Kant, for identifying the thing-in-itself with Will. Is this, as Russell suggests, a more defensible development of Kant than the alternative moves made by Fichte and Hegel?
rubric: Accurately reconstructs the Kantian premises Schopenhauer relies on
Explains why the Will must be single and timeless on this view
Compares fairly with Fichte's/Hegel's alternative response to Kant

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's two distinct criticisms of Schopenhauer's doctrine of ascetic salvation: the philosophical criticism (that its goal is incoherently negative) and the biographical criticism (that Schopenhauer's own life contradicted his preaching). Are these independent objections, and does either succeed on its own?
rubric: Clearly distinguishes the philosophical from the biographical objection
Explains each objection accurately with textual support
Considers whether a hypocrite's doctrine can still be true/coherent
